description: We are a team based in Dhaka, We are aimed for making a ground breaking innovation in Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data based on provided NASA data and local available real time analysis
summary:
Farmers around Ashulia mostly grow Boro rice in the dry season and Aman rice in the monsoon, with the land empty in between. Boro needs a great deal of pumped groundwater, and it flowers in March–April, which is the hottest part of the year. NASA POWER shows about 16 days at or above 35 °C in March–April at this location today. The NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 futures we tested put that at roughly 24 to 40 days by the 2030s and 2050s. Rice flowering is sensitive to heat above about 35 °C.

Furrow takes a farmer from "where is my field" to "which rotation should I follow, and what do I do this season" in a few minutes. The farmer marks the field on a satellite map and answers 18 short questions about crops, land, water, soil and priorities. Furrow then scores five candidate rotations, including the farmer's current one, against 13 climate futures: the observed 2001–2025 climate plus 12 model futures (three CMIP6 models × SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 × 2030s and 2050s). It recommends the rotation with the smallest worst-case regret. With equal priorities that is Mustard → Mungbean → T. Aman. In the observed climate it needs about 530 mm of irrigation a year, against about 1,210 mm for the current Boro – Fallow – T. Aman. It also puts a nitrogen-fixing legume into the rotation and gives the hottest months to mungbean, which tolerates more heat than Boro. The runner-up is Maize → Mungbean → T. Aman. If the farmer changes their priorities, the ranking changes with them.
details:
Project details: Furrow

What it does
Furrow is a mobile decision-support app for one farmer and one field. It answers one question: which crop rotation should this field follow for the next few years, given how its climate has already changed and how it is likely to change next? It combines three NASA datasets with the field's soil, the characteristics of each crop and the farmer's own priorities. It recommends the rotation that stays close to the best choice in every climate future tested, not the one that wins in only one.

How it works

  1. Mark the field. The farmer finds their village, taps the field's corners on a satellite map (area shown in decimals and bigha), and answers 18 short picture-based questions about crops, land, water, soil and priorities.
  2. History. NASA POWER daily data, 1996–2026, gives heat days (≥ 35 °C and ≥ 38 °C), cold nights (< 15 °C), heavy-rain days, dry spells and reference evapotranspiration (FAO-56 Hargreaves).
  3. Futures. NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 changes from three models (ACCESS-CM2, MIROC6, MRI-ESM2-0) under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5, for the 2030s and 2050s, are applied to the observed 2001–2025 days. That gives 12 futures, 13 including the observed climate.
    • climate stress at each crop's sensitive stage
    • water need (FAO-56)
    • soil health (cover, legumes, crop families, no rice after rice)
    • illustrative income
  4. Decision. The farmer's priorities weight the scores. Furrow recommends the rotation with the smallest worst-case regret and shows the runner-up.

Result for the pilot field (Ashulia, Savar, Dhaka, Bangladesh)

  • Today about 16 days ≥ 35 °C in March–April, when Boro rice flowers. Futures put it at about 24–40 days by the 2030s–2050s.
  • With equal priorities, the recommendation is Mustard → Mungbean → T. Aman: about 530 mm of irrigation a year against about 1,210 mm for the current Boro – Fallow – T. Aman. It adds a nitrogen-fixing legume and gives the hottest months to heat-tolerant mungbean. The runner-up is Maize → Mungbean → T. Aman.

What the farmer sees

  • Home: field status, crop health from satellite (MODIS greenness against the normal), top warnings, jobs to do now.
  • Alerts: flood, heavy rain, heat, drought, cold, dry spells, waterlogging and pests, each with an action. Includes a 12-month risk calendar and a 7-day forecast.
  • Advice: recommended rotation and runner-up, risk in a bad year, a soil-nutrient plan (BARC 2018), all rotations compared, and the season's to-do list.
  • History: 30 years of big events, heat, rain, soil moisture, crop health, and future climate as ranges.
  • Drone: request a drone check of the field (survey maps in the app are demo data for now).
  • Works offline: NASA data is bundled in the app.

NASA data

  • NASA POWER daily point API: weather, rain and soil wetness, 1996–2026.
  • MODIS MOD13Q1 v061 NDVI, 250 m: crop greenness, 2000–2026.
  • NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, 0.25°: daily max temperature and rainfall projections.

Benefits

  • Less pumped groundwater.
  • Healthier soil through legumes and crop diversity.
  • Less heat risk at flowering.
  • Warnings with clear actions.
  • Every projection is shown as a range with its scenario named. Furrow is decision support, not a forecast.

What we checked and what we don't claim

  • Two data issues found and handled:
    • POWER runs 2–4 °C warmer than bias-corrected CMIP6 in March–May here, so it's adjusted month by month.
    • POWER rainfall jumps in 2017, so trends use 1996–2016 only.
  • Machine learning tested: regression models trained on NASA data didn't beat a "normal year" baseline, so the app uses none.
  • Limits: crop prices are illustrative, and the CMIP6 sample is small.

Future development

  • More CMIP6 models with full 30-year windows.
  • SMAP soil moisture and GPM IMERG rainfall.
  • Backtesting against yields.
  • A Bangla version with voice.
  • Real drone canopy maps on a 5 m grid.
  • Local market prices.
  • New regions across South Asia, which need no new data infrastructure because all the NASA data is global.
  • A season-long pilot with extension officers.

Tools and technology

  • Languages: TypeScript (app), Python (data pipelines), SQL (database).
  • Software: Expo SDK 58, React Native, React 19, Leaflet 1.9, d3, Supabase (optional).
  • Map and other data: Esri World Imagery, OpenStreetMap (Nominatim place search), Open-Meteo forecast.
  • Hardware: the team's own prototype drone (shown in the demo video).

Links

  • Web app: https://ratul-islam.github.io/Furrow/
  • Code and Android app: https://github.com/Ratul-islam/Furrow
  • Licence: Apache 2.0
